selected.headline: 24-Hour Economy targets 30,000 jobs with pharmaceutical park at Ningo Prampram …Today is deadline for drugmakers to register interest
selected.evidence: The government has opened registration for pharmaceutical manufacturers to establish operations in the Legon Pharmaceutical Innovation Park (LePIP), a 2,000-acre facility planned at Ningo Prampram in the Greater Accra Region. The project, being developed by the 24-Hour Economy and Accelerated Export Development (24H+) Authority with the Ghana Infrastructure and Investment Fund (GIIF), is expected to create wealth and an estimated 30,000 jobs, according to the Authority. Companies have until today (October 12) to submit expressions of interest. About 70 per cent of Ghana’s pharmaceutical demand is met through imports, costing the country more than $300 million annually, the call for expressions of interest says. The government has set a target of replacing 50 per cent of imports with locally produced medicines by 2030. The Authority describes LePIP as Ghana’s first integrated pharmaceutical innovation park, designed to make the country a manufacturing and export hub for West Africa and beyond. Under the plan, a special purpose vehicle will provide shared infrastructure, including power, water and steam meeting Good Manufacturing Practice (GMP) standards, an effluent treatment plant, cold-chain warehousing and ready-built factory shells. Quality control laboratories, supervised by the University of Ghana, and a research centre focused on tropical diseases will also be provided. Tenants will pay fees or lease charges for these services. Companies producing active pharmaceutical ingredients, generics, vaccines, herbal medicines and diagnostics are eligible. Joint ventures and consortia may apply. Anchor tenants may be offered equity in the special purpose vehicle, subject to final terms. The Authority stresses that the exercise is not a tender and confers no lease, award or equity right. Shortlisted firms will be invited to bilateral discussions from October 26 this year. The UK-funded Ghana Jobs and Economic Transformation (JET) Programme is supporting the process.

selected.headline: Syria issues first letter of credit to Saudi Aramco in 14 years | The Jerusalem Post
selected.evidence: Syria's central bank said on Sunday it issued its first letter of credit in 14 years to facilitate a petroleum products supply deal between the Syrian Petroleum Company and Saudi Aramco (2222.SE).The bank said the transaction was arranged in coordination with a major US bank, which it did not name, opening a channel to finance oil imports and settle payments through the formal banking system.The move marks a step toward restoring Syria's access to international banking channels following the removal of US sanctions and its designation as a state sponsor of terrorism.Saudi Arabia's energy minister signed three memorandums of understanding with Kuwait, Qatar and Egypt to strengthen energy cooperation, the Saudi state news agency said on Sunday.The agreement with Qatar sets a framework for collaboration in petroleum, natural gas and petrochemicals, including exploring joint opportunities to develop pipelines for transport and exports.Syria no longer classified as state sponsor of terrorismThe United States officially removed Syria from its list of state sponsors of terrorism at the end of August. Damascus claimed at the time that the step was the last major impediment for the country to bring in foreign investment.Syrian Foreign Minister Asaad Al-Shibani told Reuters that the government hoped removing what he called the "last obstacle" would help reconnect Syria to the global financial and economic system and boost investment. "There is no longer any obstacle to investment, doing business and rebuilding economic life in Syria," he said.“These actions were all taken in recognition of the positive actions taken and further commitments by the Syrian government under President Ahmed Al-Sharaa to fully distance Syria from acts of international terrorism,” US Secretary of State Marco Rubio said in a statement.Syria had been on the list since 1979, when Washington accused the government of former President Hafez al-Assad of supporting militant groups. The designation remained throughout the rule of his son Bashar Al-Assad, who was toppled by rebels led by current President Ahmed Al-Sharaa in December 2024.

selected.headline: Roman fort found in Wales could prove myth of emperor’s camp is real
selected.evidence: Exclusive: Finds suggest account in medieval folklore of a camp near Frenni Fawr hill was rooted in reality Exclusive: Finds suggest account in medieval folklore of a camp near Frenni Fawr hill was rooted in reality Magnus Maximus, the Roman emperor who ruled Britain in the fourth century, led his troops against the Picts and Scots, but a theory that he also established a military camp near Frenni Fawr hill in Wales has so far been based on folklore. Now fourth-century coins, among other finds at a newly identified Roman fort in Pembrokeshire, suggest the medieval tale was rooted in reality, to the excitement of archaeologists. The fort was discovered by Dr Mark Merrony, a leading Roman specialist at the University of Oxford. He heads an excavation that is bringing to life a story about Magnus Maximus, as told in the Mabinogion, a collection of medieval epic tales of myth, magic and miracles. Merrony expressed excitement that this landscape held the only Roman military site close to where the Mabinogion places the emperor. “If Magnus Maximus was there, there must have been an army there,” he said. “It’s such a remote area but the tale mentions the easternmost peak of the Preseli Hills, which is where this site is. The presence of a heavily fortified Roman auxiliary fort may help unlock the mystery of a Mabinogion legend that has endured for nearly 1,700 years.” In The Dream of Macsen Wledig , medieval storytellers used the emperor’s name in Welsh in recounting his rise to power. They described how on his military manoeuvres, he pitched his camp at Frenni Fawr, the 395-metre (1,300ft) easternmost peak of the Preseli Hills. There had been no archaeological evidence for a Roman marching camp or fort on the summit of the Frenni Fawr or below it until now. Merrony discovered it about 2 miles (3.5km) south-west of the summit in 2024. Satellite imagery had shown a convincing outline in an overgrown field and, shortly after visiting it, his eye was caught by a Roman tile, which turned out to be the first of many. With financial support from Oxford University and crowdfunding, one of several planned excavations has just finished, confirming his theory of the site and its significance. Merrony said that before the dig, his brother, Nick, had jokingly asked him to find a couple of coins to prove the Magnus Maximus theory. “He came back and said ‘well, are these any good?’ I said ‘you’ve got to be kidding me’. He’d found two coins dating from the late 4th century. “It is fascinating to consider that the two coins may be linked to the tale of Macsen Wledig – Magnus Maximus – in the Mabinogion, the Welsh equivalent of the Odyssey.” Merrony is a leading specialist in the Romano-British period. His previous discoveries include two Roman villas, at Ford in Pembrokeshire and at Cutteslowe in Oxfordshire. He identified a Roman road along the southern shoulder of the Preselis in 2022, challenging assumptions that the Romans did not venture far into Wales. His research will appear in Antiqvvs , a quarterly magazine dedicated to archaeology, ancient art and history. Magnus Maximus will also feature in Merrony’s forthcoming book, titled Lives of the Roman Emperors: From Augustus to Romulus Augustulus . Our morning email breaks down the key stories of the day, telling you what’s happening and why it matters Measuring 180 by 150 metres, the fort is on a slope with a commanding view of the surrounding landscape. It is likely to have held about 500 troops, and its discovery overturns assumptions that the area’s Indigenous Celtic tribe was on peaceful terms with the Roman invaders. It has “a characteristic playing-card form, with rounded corners” and a perpendicular road, Merrony said. Finds at the site so far include an unusual iron stylus, many pottery shards, large quantities of Roman tiles and extensive compacted clay floors, a common feature on Roman military sites. Even rut marks left by wagons have been preserved. The geophysical survey confirmed the presence of a rectangular building in the middle of the enclosure and a larger rectangular building immediately to the south. “This arrangement is consistent with the placement of a headquarters building orientated east and thereby ‘facing the enemy’, and a commander’s house,” Merrony said.

selected.headline: World Bank jobs council urges 'crisis-era' employment support measures as IMF warns of AI ‘tsunami’
selected.evidence: BANGKOK — Policymakers are moving from debating whether artificial intelligence will hit jobs to issuing stark warnings about AI-led disruption and recommending measures on cushioning the fallout. International Monetary Fund Managing Director Kristalina Georgieva warned on Monday that artificial intelligence was hitting the global labor market like a "slow-moving tsunami," with young graduates first in line to be knocked down. "People to worry about, first and foremost, [are] young people that are coming into the labor market," Georgieva said at a panels on Monday. "Normally, they would get into these routine, repetitive jobs and then grow up the ranks. But if they're gone, I don't think any young person wants to be a barista in a coffee shop as ... professional future." Speaking on the same panel, Singapore President Tharman Shanmugaratnam, who co-chairs the World Bank's Jobs Council, called for governments to make "crisis-era" support measures a permanent tool for getting young people into work. What governments did during the Covid-19 pandemic and, in some cases, the global financial crisis "now has to be thought of not as a crisis measure, but as part of the structural, the menu of structural policies," he said. That means working with the private sector, and incentivizing firms to hire fresh graduates, because "the first rung in employment, your first job upon graduation, is now seeing less demand," Shanmugaratnam said. The remarks show that policymakers are moving from debating whether AI will disrupt jobs to deciding how to cushion the fallout, at a time when rapidly aging populations, particularly in Asia, already threaten to shrink workforces. World Bank President Ajay Banga, estimates 1.2 billion young people will turn 18 over the next 15 years, and the private sector, which already generates 75% to 85% of jobs in any country, will have to absorb most of them. Governments' role is to make that possible, he said, by building infrastructure, setting policy and "de-risking" private capital, or lowering the risks that deter investors from putting in money at scale. "It is private capital that creates jobs," he said. The IMF estimates that about 40% of jobs worldwide will eventually be "augmented, downgraded or eliminated." Exposure is about 60% in advanced economies and 23% in low-income countries, she said, but poorer nations are not better off: that is "just because AI is further away." The squeeze is clearest in tech, Shanmugaratnam said, adding that in the U.S. "for the first time in a century, demand for graduates has gone down," with the wage premium for a college degree also shrinking. Without action, a cohort of graduates loses more than a year of skills: "you lose trust in the future," he said. AI has also been the major driver propping up growth this year. AI-related investments and trade have lifted output in a handful of economies, helping keep global expansion near 3% despite an energy supply shock, Georgieva said. "Love it, hate it, or fear it. It [AI] is here, and we are already seeing the first wave of impact," Georgieva said, estimating AI adoption could lift growth by 0.5 percentage point to 1 percentage point in advanced Asia, and 0.2 percentage point to 0.8 percentage point in emerging Asia. At the high end, that "would more than offset the loss that comes from aging population," said Georgieva. Shanmugaratnam cautioned that growth alone may not necessarily deliver job creation. China, India and developing Southeast Asia are "growing quite well, but job creation is weak," he said, and AI "is going to widen that divergence if we are too passive about it." AI-induced job displacement, however, will come "task by task," he said, "and that gives us time" — provided workers can learn on the job and universities shift toward applied training. selected.headline: Intensive breathwork reduces brain blood flow and alters neural communication
selected.evidence: Intensive breathing exercises can reduce blood flow to the brain by up to 45% and alter communication between brain networks, according to a new brain-imaging study. Participants reported experiences resembling some effects of psychedelic drugs, including altered perception, vivid mental imagery, a sense of unity and changes in self-experience. The researchers, presenting the work at the ECNP Congress in Munich, say changes in brain communication, rather than reduced blood flow alone, appear to be key to the altered state. The study involved 30 healthy, experienced breathwork practitioners who performed high-ventilation breathwork during MRI scanning. Participants reported strong altered states of consciousness, describing a predominantly oceanic state – in other words, a deep feeling of connection to the universe - resembling that of a moderate to high dose of LSD or psilocybin, albeit with less pronounced visual effects. Brain imaging showed that global grey-matter cerebral blood flow fell by around 45% during the session, on average from 16.24 to 9.81 ml/100g/min. Those who reported stronger altered states also showed greater changes in the brain's default mode network, which is involved in self-reflection and self-related thinking. The researchers suggest that the intensity of the experience is not simply explained by reduced blood flow. Instead, the experience might track more closely with changes in communication within the default mode network, a brain system linked to self-reflection and self-related thought. Lead researcher Dr Christian Schmitz, Central Institute of Mental Health, Mannheim in Germany, said: " Many people who practice intensive breathwork report profound changes in perception and self-experience, yet the underlying brain mechanisms remain poorly understood. Our study suggests that these experiences are linked not only to marked changes in cerebral blood flow, but also to alterations in how key brain networks communicate". 'Co-Coordinator, Hana Adolphi said, " Breathwork is a legal, inexpensive and non-pharmacological intervention that may provide a valuable tool for studying altered states of consciousness. Understanding these mechanisms could also help inform future research into novel approaches for mental health treatment. Nevertheless, this was a relatively small study, and the findings should be considered preliminary. Larger studies will be needed to determine whether these brain changes have clinical relevance." Commenting, Dr Guy Fincham (Brighton and Sussex Medical School, UK) said: "This study is intriguing as it is starting to extend findings from recent breathwork research that intensive breathing practices may yield altered states of consciousness which individuals describe in ways analogous to psychedelic compounds, and under brain-imaging conditions. These findings are important because such altered subjective experiences may be harnessed for the improvement of mental health, and an accessible non-pharmacological route such a breathwork could prove invaluable for many. We should note that the study was uncontrolled and the sample was made up of experienced practitioners, so replication of this in breathwork-naïve participants using a randomised-controlled design will help determine whether these findings can translate more widely and produce therapeutic benefit". Dr Fincham was not involved in this study; this is an independent comment. Professor David Nutt (of Imperial College, London) said: "Breathwork is a non-pharmacological bridge to our research into psychedelics, so research which helps us understand how it functions is welcome". Professor Nutt was not involved in this study; this is an independent comment.
